transcript: I don't know I mean I think One problem with saying that nursing homes are infrastructure is that there's a different pay for more subsidies for nursing homes than there would be for a long-term capital project like a bridge that might last 50 years. And I think it's appropriate to pay for that kind of a bridge. And we just built one in Cleveland recently. Took us about 20 years to do it. You need to increase that gas tax or do something else because that wouldn't be enough. I prefer just to index that gas tax going forward. So not increase it. So I think there's some combination of things like that that can be used. The Biden administration idea was to raise taxes. The problem with the taxes they want to raise is it would hurt You know, the very competitiveness we finally have in this country where it's not a disadvantage to be an American company. You know, we had two great Cleveland companies, you know, choose to invert a few years ago, meaning they became foreign companies just to get out from under our tax code. And they did that because our tax code was so uncompetitive. And what the Biden administration wants to do is make us uncompetitive again by raising our taxes, which according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, for its workers, more than anyone else, they say 70% of the benefit of the corporate tax reforms went to workers, and if you do the opposite, the same would be true, you'd be hurting workers. And wages, and we saw this, we saw wages going up pre-pandemic, February of last year was the 19th straight month of wage gains of over 3% annualized, which I love, and we loved it in Northeast Ohio, because we finally were seeing real wages above inflation. So that's the danger. The taxes, Dan, I will tell you that the Biden folks proposed, and I don't know if this was a serious proposal or if it was just to sort of get a big proposal out there, $2.4 trillion in these big tax increases, but the tax increases were five times higher than the tax cuts. for the same businesses in 2017. In other words, it wasn't just reversing what we did in 2017 and making our US companies less competitive again. It was actually adding new taxes on top of that. And we can send you all the joint tax committee analysis of that. It's a non-partisan analysis. But that just doesn't make any sense right now as we're trying to be more competitive. At the same time, we were working on a bill on the House and Senate floor right now that has to do with being more competitive, particularly vis-a-vis China. Well, part of the way you're competitive is you have a tax structure that makes your businesses and your workers competitive. So anyway, that's my concern with it. Having said that, I think we can get to a bipartisan compromise here because I think we're starting to define it closer to what is real infrastructure. The apples to apples comparison is about 600 billion on the Republican side. Again, I'm pressing in an amount by any Republican or Democrat proposal in the past, and the Democrat proposal with the Biden administration for the same type of infrastructure, you know, real infrastructure would be about $900 billion. And although $300 billion sounds like a lot of money, and it is, it used to be a lot of money in this town, I think we could bridge that gap in part by using some of this creative financing that you use with regard to longer-term capital expenses.
